summary: Teach stellar nucleosynthesis ('we are made of star-stuff') for ages 12–14 as a causal sequence of cosmic 'factories': the Big Bang made only the lightest elements (hydrogen, helium, a trace of lithium); stars fuse hydrogen to helium and, in massive stars, climb a ladder of heavier nuclei (carbon, oxygen, silicon) but only up to IRON; fusing anything heavier than iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it, so fusion stalls at the 'iron wall' and the massive star's core collapses; elements heavier than iron are built by neutron capture rather than energy-releasing fusion — some slowly inside ageing giant stars, and the heaviest (such as gold and uranium) mainly in neutron-star mergers and possibly rare kinds of supernova; stellar winds, supernovae and mergers scatter these elements into space to seed new stars and planets. The unifying idea is cosmic recycling, with the periodic table as a map of where each element was born. The load-bearing insight is the energy turning point at iron, which explains both why stars cannot build gold by fusion and why massive stars collapse and explode.
misconceptions: 'All elements were made in the Big Bang' — only hydrogen, helium and a little lithium; everything else came later from stars
'Stars can fuse any element to keep shining' — fusion only releases energy up to iron; beyond iron it absorbs energy, which is why iron is the endpoint
'The Sun will make gold' — low-mass stars like the Sun stop at carbon/oxygen; heavy elements need supernovae or neutron-star mergers
'Elements made in stars stay locked inside them' — stellar winds and especially supernova explosions scatter them into space to form new stars and planets
'Supernovae only destroy' — they are also the forges and distributors of the heavy elements essential to planets and life
'Nuclear fusion and chemical reactions are the same' — forming elements changes atomic nuclei (protons/neutrons), not just how atoms bond

activities.title: Run a star: the element staircase and the iron wall
steps: Start from hydrogen and fuse it to helium, then climb the staircase to carbon, oxygen and silicon, watching an energy-out indicator glow positive at each step.

Notice that the energy return shrinks as you approach iron; then try to fuse one step past iron and observe the energy indicator flip negative (fusing beyond iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it).

Observe the core collapse and supernova that follows the iron wall, and watch elements made in the star and in the explosion (including some heavier than iron, which were not produced in the earlier energy-releasing fusion steps) scattered into a nebula that will form new planets; note that scientists still debate how much gold and uranium ordinary supernovae make.
Use a mass dial to re-run the star as a low-mass, Sun-like star that ends gently at carbon/oxygen without forging the heaviest elements, then as a massive star that reaches iron and explodes.
Optionally trigger a neutron-star merger event to see additional heavy (r-process) elements such as gold formed by a separate pathway.
Finish by mapping elements in your own body (calcium in bones, iron in blood) to the cosmic factory where each was made.
activities.insight: Fusion releases energy only up to iron; beyond iron it costs energy, so iron is the endpoint of energy-releasing stellar fusion — and that energy wall, not merely 'running out of fuel', is why massive stars collapse and why elements beyond iron must be built another way (neutron capture), with the heaviest, such as gold and uranium, coming mainly from neutron-star mergers and possibly rare supernovae.

activities.title: The periodic table as a map of cosmic origins
steps: Explore a periodic table colour-coded by origin (Big Bang, dying low-mass stars, exploding massive stars, neutron-star mergers, cosmic-ray spallation).
Tap or select individual elements to reveal where each was forged and an everyday or body example (e.g. oxygen you breathe, iron in your blood, gold in a ring).
Open the entry for iron to read why it is the 'end of the line' for energy-releasing fusion.
Trace the cosmic-recycling loop in the legend: nebula → star → supernova → enriched nebula → next star and planet.
activities.insight: The periodic table is a map of cosmic origins: different elements were born in different processes, and the same recycling loop links stellar life and death to the raw material of new worlds and living things.

activities.title: Sort, sequence and explain: consolidation check
steps: Sort elements (e.g. H, He, C, O, Fe, Au) into their birthplaces: Big Bang, stellar fusion, supernova/neutron-star merger.
Put the fusion ladder in order from hydrogen up to iron.
Answer and justify: why can't an ordinary star fuse past iron to release energy, and where do elements heavier than iron come from?
activities.insight: Consolidate the chapters of the story — Big Bang light elements, fusion up to iron, supernovae/mergers for the heaviest — and check that the iron limit is understood as an energy reversal, not just exhausted fuel.

activities.title: Ask the astrophysicist: how do we know?
steps: Discuss with (or role-play) a nuclear astrophysicist the 'you are stardust' story, asking how scientists know the gold in a ring came from an exploding star or a neutron-star collision.
Pose follow-up questions about evidence, such as how the 2017 gravitational-wave observation linked a neutron-star merger to heavy-element formation.
Explain back, in your own words, why iron is the endpoint and how your body's atoms trace to earlier stars.
activities.insight: Scientific claims about element origins rest on evidence (binding-energy physics, supernova observations, gravitational-wave detections), and learners can articulate both the story and how we know it.

checkQuestion: The carbon and oxygen atoms in your body, and the iron in your blood — where were they actually made? Was it all in the Big Bang, or here on Earth when the planet formed? And a puzzle: why does an ordinary star build elements only up to IRON, and where do heavier elements like gold and uranium come from? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: The Big Bang made almost only the lightest elements — hydrogen and helium. Everything heavier was forged later inside stars, not on Earth. Nuclear fusion in stars builds progressively heavier elements, releasing energy, up to IRON. Iron is the stopping point because fusing iron does NOT release energy — it absorbs it — so the star can no longer support itself, its core collapses, and it explodes as a supernova. Elements heavier than iron, such as gold and uranium, are made in those violent supernovae (and neutron-star collisions), which also scatter all these elements into space, where they become the raw material for new stars, planets and living things. So the atoms in your body were literally made in ancient stars.
